title: Joy to the world
hookLine: Isaac Watts wrote it as a psalm (Psalm 98), not originally for Christmas

lines: A CAROL IN A GROCERY STORE.
cards: A carol plays in a grocery store in December, between the canned cranberries and the wrapping paper. Joy to the world, the Lord is come. It gets filed under Christmas.
Now listen to the words. No manger, no shepherds, no star, no wise men, no baby at all. There's earth, heaven, fields and floods, rocks, hills and plains, and a king who rules the world.
It reads less like a nativity scene than a coronation. That's because it began as something else.

teach.h: THE PSALMS, SUNG WITH JESUS IN VIEW.
teach.b: Isaac Watts was an English minister among the Dissenters, the Protestants outside the Church of England. In his day, some of those churches sang only the Psalms, in versions kept close to the Bible's wording.
Watts thought Christians should sing the Psalms the way a Christian would pray them, with Jesus in view. So he rewrote the Psalms in his own verse, and Joy to the world is his version of Psalm 98.
Open the King James Bible to that psalm and you can hear the bones of the hymn: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all the earth: make a loud noise, and rejoice, and sing praise."

A little further, the sea roars, the floods clap their hands, the hills are joyful together. Why? Because the Lord comes to judge the earth: "with righteousness shall he judge the world, and the people with equity."
Watts opened his hymn: "Joy to the world! the Lord is come; Let earth receive her King." For Watts the coming king is Jesus, and the hymn looks toward his rule over all the earth.

Christians read that coming more than one way. Some hear the first coming, the birth, which is why it found a home at Christmas. Others hear the coming at the end of the age, when the world is set right.
Watts didn't write it for any one season. And look at the line that becomes ours. Let earth receive her king.
Not the church, not the good people. The earth: fields and floods, rocks and hills.
The whole created world is invited to make room.

how: Joy to the World is sung in Protestant and Catholic churches, usually at Christmas, though some churches also sing it in Advent or at other seasons as a hymn of Christ's rule.

games.q: you're Isaac Watts. your church sings the Psalms word for word, but you want Christians to sing them with Jesus in view. what do you do?
o: stop singing the Psalms at all.
rewrite the Psalms in your own verse.
games.why: Watts rewrote the Psalms in his own verse. Joy to the world is his Psalm 98, with no manger in it at all.

practice: Out of season is the point: say to yourself what today actually is, an ordinary day with no tinsel, and sing the first line into it, quietly or out loud.

Then let the psalm's list go by in your mind, one at a time: the sea, the floods, the hills. If you pray, make the last line yours, let earth receive her king; if you don't, notice the earth under you, holding you up.
